title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Faunal Diversity — 2024
subject: biology
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Write the diagnostic features of the phylum Arthropoda. Give one example.
questions.solution:
Jointed appendages; **chitinous exoskeleton**; segmented body (head–thorax–abdomen); open circulation; tracheal/gill respiration.

Example: *Periplaneta* (cockroach), prawn, king crab — the largest animal phylum (~75% of known species are insects).
questions.knowledgeNote: Moulting (ecdysis) is the price of armour — growth happens only between sheds.
questions.answer: **Diagnostic features of Arthropoda:** jointed paired appendages; chitinous exoskeleton (moulted to grow); segmented body (head/thorax/abdomen or cephalothorax/abdomen); open circulatory system with dorsal heart; compound eyes; ventral nerve cord; largest phylum. **Example:** housefly (*Musca*) — or prawn, crab, butterfly. **Deep point:** 'jointed feet' is the literal name and the defining engineering — armour plus articulated joints made land colonisation possible.

questions.question: Describe the respiratory system of frog.
questions.solution:
**Cutaneous** (moist skin — underwater/hibernation), **buccal** (mouth-cavity pumping), **pulmonary** (paired sac-like lungs on land).

Frogs ventilate by **positive pressure**: mouth fills with air, nostrils shut, buccal floor forces air into the lungs.
questions.knowledgeNote: Tadpoles breathe with gills — metamorphosis rebuilds the whole respiratory toolkit.
questions.answer: **Respiratory system of the frog (three modes):** **(1) Cutaneous** — thin, moist, vascular skin; O₂ dissolves in mucus and diffuses into blood (main mode in water and at rest). **(2) Buccopharyngeal** — moist vascular lining of the mouth; rhythmic raising/lowering of the buccal floor ventilates it (nostrils open, mouth shut). **(3) Pulmonary** — a pair of simple sac-like lungs via glottis and laryngotracheal chamber; **positive-pressure ventilation**: nostrils close, buccal floor rises and forces ('swallows') air into the lungs; used mainly on land and during activity. **Deep point:** skin for water, lungs for land, mouth lining always — the frog's triple kit is its double life made anatomy.

questions.question: Write the general characters of phylum Mollusca with two examples.
questions.solution:
Soft unsegmented body in three parts (head – visceral mass – muscular foot); usually a calcareous **shell**; mantle cavity with gills; open circulation (except cephalopods).

Examples: *Pila* (apple snail), *Unio* (freshwater mussel), octopus.
questions.knowledgeNote: Second-largest phylum — pearls are nacre-coated irritants, the oyster's defence turned luxury.
questions.answer: **General characters of Mollusca:** (1) **soft-bodied, unsegmented** (second largest phylum); (2) **muscular foot** for locomotion (or tentacles in cephalopods); (3) a **visceral hump** covered by a **mantle** which usually secretes a **calcareous shell** (absent/reduced in some); (4) open circulatory system (closed in cephalopods) with a dorsal heart; (5) respiration by **gills (ctenidia)** or lungs (pulmonates); (6) radula (rasping organ) in the mouth of most; (7) separate sexes or hermaphrodite; aquatic mostly, some terrestrial. **Two examples:** ***Pila*** (apple snail), ***Unio*** (freshwater mussel) — also octopus, slug, oyster. **Deep point:** foot, mantle, shell — three words carry the whole phylum; the mantle's secretion is the pearl-making machinery too.

questions.question: Distinguish between chordates and non-chordates.
questions.solution:
**Chordates** have (at some stage) a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, and a post-anal tail — e.g. fish, frog, humans.

**Non-chordates** lack all four — e.g. earthworm, snail, starfish. Chordates are mostly bilateral with closed circulation; non-chordates far more diverse in symmetry and systems.
questions.knowledgeNote: Human gill slits appear only as embryos — ontogeny briefly replays phylogeny.
questions.answer: **Chordates vs non-chordates:** **(1) Notochord:** chordates possess a **notochord** (rod of cells below the nerve cord; replaced by the vertebral column in vertebrates) at some stage; non-chordates never have one. **(2) Nerve cord:** chordates have a **dorsal, hollow, single nerve cord**; non-chordates have a **ventral, solid, double** nerve cord (e.g. annelids, arthropods). **(3) Pharyngeal gill slits:** present in chordates at some stage of life; absent in non-chordates. **(4) Tail:** chordates have a **post-anal tail**; non-chordates do not. **(5) Heart:** chordate heart is **ventral** (below the gut); non-chordate heart (where present) is **dorsal**. **Examples:** chordates — frog, fish, man; non-chordates — earthworm, housefly, starfish. **Deep point:** the four chordate marks (notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail) appear at least embryonically in every chordate — the human embryo still has gill slits and a tail; the features are a developmental signature, not just adult anatomy.

questions.question: Write the general characters of phylum Annelida with one example.
questions.solution:
True segmentation (**metamerism**), closed circulation, setae/chaetae for movement, moist cuticle, hermaphroditic.

Example: *Pheretima* (earthworm) — the soil's ploughman.
questions.knowledgeNote: Metamerism (repeated segments) prefigures the vertebrate backbone's serial plan.
questions.answer: **General characters of Annelida:** (1) **true segmented worms** — body divided externally and internally into ring-like **metameres** (annulus = ring); (2) **triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical, truly coelomate** (first true coelom in evolution); (3) closed circulatory system; (4) **nephridia** as excretory organs; (5) respiration through moist skin (cutaneous); (6) setae (in earthworm) or parapodia (in Nereis) for locomotion; hermaphrodite in earthworm/leech. **One example:** ***Pheretima posthuma*** (earthworm) — also *Hirudinaria* (leech), *Nereis*. **Deep point:** 'ringed' is the name and the plan — segmentation is the annelid's signature invention, later inherited by arthropods and chordates.

questions.question: What is the water vascular system? In which phylum is it found? Write its functions.
questions.solution:
Found in **Echinodermata** (starfish): seawater-filled canals ending in suckered **tube feet**, worked by ampullae.

Functions: locomotion, food capture, respiration, and excretion — hydraulics instead of muscles.
questions.knowledgeNote: Radial symmetry in adults but bilateral larvae — echinoderms evolved *back* to radial from bilateral ancestors.
questions.answer: **Water vascular system:** a unique **hydraulic system of fluid-filled canals** — ring canal around the mouth → radial canals → **tube feet** (podia) with muscular ampullae and suckered tips; sea water enters through a madreporite plate and circulates through the canals. **Phylum:** **Echinodermata** (starfish *Asterias*, sea urchin, sea cucumber) — found in no other phylum. **Functions:** (1) **locomotion** — muscles squeeze the ampulla to extend the tube foot, relax to retract, so the animal 'steps' on its tube feet; (2) **food capture and handling** — tube feet pry open bivalve shells; (3) **respiration and excretion** — diffusion through the thin tube-foot walls; (4) **sensory/attachment** — gripping substrates. **Deep point:** the system is a hydraulic skeleton and muscle in one — no other phylum solved locomotion with pressurised sea water, which is why echinoderms are radially symmetrical yet still mobile.
